title: New Headache During a Blood Transfusion (Assessing a Transfusion Reaction)
patient_instructions: You are a 68-year-old woman currently receiving a blood transfusion for anaemia when a new headache started. If asked: this is the FIRST time you have ever had a headache like this; it is a dull, band-like tightening across your head, moderate in severity. You feel a little anxious. Give these answers only if the candidate asks specifically - you feel a bit short of breath and warm/flushed, you have had some chills; you have NO rash, NO itch, NO chest pain, NO noisy breathing or throat tightness. You are being transfused because you were told you are anaemic; you have had one previous transfusion without problems. You take no regular painkillers. You are under some stress caring for your husband. Ideas: 'Is the blood not agreeing with me?' Concerns: you are worried something is going wrong with the transfusion. Expectations: you want it checked and to feel safe. Appear mildly distressed and keep touching your head.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor on the ward of a rural district hospital. A 68-year-old woman receiving a blood transfusion for anaemia develops a new headache. In 8 minutes: take a focused history to determine the cause, state the examination findings you would look for, and give your leading assessment. Prioritise safety - explain any immediate actions aloud.
examiner_instructions: The key insight is that the headache is a possible sign of a TRANSFUSION REACTION, not an isolated headache. Reward the candidate who first asks 'Is this the first time you have had such a headache?' and who, on suspecting a reaction, states they would STOP the transfusion immediately, keep IV access open with normal saline and reassess ABC before continuing the history. Award marks for screening reaction types: acute haemolytic (ABO) reaction, anaphylaxis, TRALI, TACO, septic/bacterial contamination and febrile non-haemolytic reaction. If asked for examination: mild fever and chills, mild breathlessness, no rash or stridor, raised JVP not present, chest clear. Candidate should re-check patient identity/labels, return the unit and giving set to the blood bank, and send appropriate bloods. Distinguish TACO (hypertension, raised JVP, responds to diuretic) from TRALI (hypotension, hypoxia). Mark communication for calm reassurance of an anxious patient.

criteria: Recognises the transfusion context and asks 'first-ever headache?' as the discriminating question
Screens reaction features: rash, itch, breathlessness, chest pain, stridor, fever/chills
Asks reason for transfusion and previous transfusion history
Briefly screens headache differentials (tension, migraine, tumour, infection)
Identifies possible transfusion reaction as the priority over benign headache
Names must-not-miss reactions (acute haemolytic/ABO, anaphylaxis, TRALI, TACO, septic)
Distinguishes TACO from TRALI on clinical features
STOPS the transfusion immediately and keeps IV access open with normal saline
Reassesses ABC and calls for help/MET as needed
Re-checks patient identity/labels; returns unit and giving set to blood bank
Sends reaction bloods (FBC, haptoglobin, LDH, bilirubin, DAT, repeat crossmatch, coagulation, cultures)
States targeted treatment (IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis; oxygen + frusemide for TACO) and haemovigilance reporting; arranges retrieval if severe
Calmly reassures and informs the anxious patient
Empathetic, structured approach appropriate to a possible emergency

red_flags: Acute haemolytic (ABO-incompatibility) reaction - fever, loin/back pain, dark urine, hypotension - stop transfusion immediately
Anaphylaxis - urticaria, angioedema, stridor, wheeze, hypotension - IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000)
TRALI - hypoxia and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6 hours, typically hypotensive
TACO - hypertension, raised JVP and pulmonary oedema from circulatory overload, responds to diuretic; and septic reaction from bacterial contamination
australian_guidelines: ANZSBT / National Blood Authority: for any suspected acute transfusion reaction STOP the transfusion immediately, maintain IV access with normal saline, reassess ABC, re-verify patient identity and labels, and return the unit and giving set to the blood bank
eTG / anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, high-flow oxygen and IV fluids for a suspected anaphylactic transfusion reaction

Reaction workup: send FBC, haptoglobin, LDH, bilirubin, direct antiglobulin test (DAT), repeat group-and-hold/crossmatch, coagulation studies and blood cultures; document and report serious reactions to the blood service (haemovigilance/Blood Watch)

TACO management: oxygen and IV frusemide (diuretic); distinguish from TRALI (hypotension, hypoxia, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema); in a rural hospital stabilise and arrange urgent retrieval if severe
learning_objectives: Interpret a new symptom during transfusion as a possible transfusion reaction
Take the first safe action - stop the transfusion, maintain IV access and reassess ABC
Recognise and differentiate the major transfusion reactions (haemolytic, anaphylaxis, TRALI, TACO, septic, febrile)
Follow Australian haemovigilance steps including identity re-check and reporting
key_points: A new symptom during a transfusion is a transfusion reaction until proven otherwise - stop the transfusion first
'Is this the first time you have had such a headache?' quickly separates a transfusion problem from a chronic headache
Re-check patient identity and unit labels and return the unit and giving set to the blood bank
TACO is hypertensive with raised JVP and responds to diuretic; TRALI is hypotensive with hypoxia within 6 hours

citations.claim: Responding calmly and empathetically to a concerned patient during a stressful transfusion follows Murtagh's communication guidance for handling anxious patients.
Framing the assessment around serious disorders not to be missed (transfusion reactions) before less urgent causes (tension headache) applies the Murtagh basic diagnostic model.
Confirming haemodynamic stability first and treating a possible reaction as time-critical reflects the safe diagnostic strategy.
